claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an epigenomic study.

claims.claim: Genetic variation in microglia may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration and AD.
claims.source: These data, together with transcriptional studies (Krasemann et al., 2017; Mathys et al., 2019; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017) support the hypothesis that genetic variation in microglia may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration and AD.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple lines of evidence from the literature.

claims.claim: Somatic genetic heterogeneity is a cause of tumoral, developmental, and immune diseases.
claims.source: Somatic genetic heterogeneity (mosaicism), resulting from post-zygotic DNA mutations, is widespread in human tissues, and a cause of tumoral, developmental, and immune diseases (Miller et al., 2021; Martincorena et al., 2015; Martincorena and Campbell, 2015; Behjati et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on somatic mosaicism.

claims.claim: The role of somatic variants in neuropsychiatric disorders is suspected.
claims.source: Additionally, the role of somatic variants in neuropsychiatric disorders is also suspected (McConnell et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claims.claim: Mosaicism has been documented in the brain tissue of AD patients in several deep-sequencing studies.
claims.source: Mosaicism has been documented in the brain tissue of AD patients in several deep-sequencing studies (Keogh et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019), showing that the enrichment of putative pathogenic somatic mutations in the PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and AMPK pathway do occur in the brain of patients in comparison to controls (Park et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to sequencing studies.

claims.claim: Enrichment of putative pathogenic somatic mutations in the PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and AMPK pathways occurs in the brain of AD patients compared to controls.
claims.source: Mosaicism has been documented in the brain tissue of AD patients in several deep-sequencing studies (Keogh et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019), showing that the enrichment of putative pathogenic somatic mutations in the PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and AMPK pathway do occur in the brain of patients in comparison to controls (Park et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific sequencing study.

claims.claim: Previous studies on somatic variants in AD brain tissue lacked cellular resolution and mechanistic insights.
claims.source: However, these studies performed in whole brain tissue lacked cellular resolution and mechanistic insights, and the role of somatic mutants in neurodegenerative diseases remains poorly understood (Miller et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior literature supported by citation.

claims.claim: Somatic variants that activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR or MAPK pathways in neural progenitors are a cause of cortical dysplasia and epilepsy.
claims.source: Somatic variants that activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR or MAPK pathways in neural progenitors are a cause of cortical dysplasia and epilepsy D'Gama et al., 2017; Khoshkhoo et al., 2023; Koh et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2015 and developmental brain malformations (Poduri et al., 2012), while somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in brain endothelial cells are associated with arteriovenous malformations (Nikolaev et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and genetic studies.

claims.claim: Somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in brain endothelial cells are associated with arteriovenous malformations.
claims.source: Somatic variants that activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR or MAPK pathways in neural progenitors are a cause of cortical dysplasia and epilepsy D'Gama et al., 2017; Khoshkhoo et al., 2023; Koh et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2015 and developmental brain malformations (Poduri et al., 2012), while somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in brain endothelial cells are associated with arteriovenous malformations (Nikolaev et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claims.claim: Expression of a somatic variant activating the MAPK pathway in microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, we reported that expression of a somatic variant activating the MAPK pathway in microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice (Mass et al., 2017), but the presence and contribution of microglial somatic clones in neurodegenerative diseases and AD remains unknown.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claims.claim: The presence and contribution of microglial somatic clones in neurodegenerative diseases and AD remains unknown.
claims.source: Interestingly, we reported that expression of a somatic variant activating the MAPK pathway in microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice (Mass et al., 2017), but the presence and contribution of microglial somatic clones in neurodegenerative diseases and AD remains unknown.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claims.claim: Human microglia develop in embryos and renew by local proliferation within the brain.
claims.source: Human microglia are reported to develop in embryos and renew by local proliferation within the brain (Askew et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017; Bian et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental biology studies.

claims.claim: Bone marrow-derived myeloid cells can enter the brain during pathological processes.
claims.source: However, bone marrow-derived myeloid cells can enter the brain, in particular during pathological processes, and may not be distinguishable from resident microglia by transcriptomics alone Kim, 2023.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: The study examined post-mortem frozen brain samples and matching blood from 45 patients with intermediate-onset sporadic AD and 44 control individuals.
claims.source: We examined post-mortem frozen brain samples and matching blood from 45 patients with intermediate-onset sporadic AD and 44 control individuals who died of other causes, including 27 donors age and sex-matched donors with the AD cohort (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the study cohort and is supported by the data in Figure 1A and supplementary materials.

claims.claim: APOE risk allele frequency for patients and controls was comparable to published series.
claims.source: APOE risk allele frequency for patients and controls was comparable to published series (Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and analysis of germline mutations did not identify deleterious variants in the 140 genes associated with neurological diseases.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Analysis of germline mutations did not identify deleterious variants in the 140 genes associated with neurological diseases.
claims.source: APOE risk allele frequency for patients and controls was comparable to published series (Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and analysis of germline mutations did not identify deleterious variants in the 140 genes associated with neurological diseases.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the genetic analysis of the cohort.

claims.claim: Approximately 94% of PU.1+ nuclei correspond to microglia.
claims.source: Single nuclei (sn)RNA-seq was performed on PU.1+ nuclei from one control and three AD patients to evaluate microglia enrichment following PU.1+ purification, and a cell-type annotation analysis indicated that ~94% of PU.1+ nuclei correspond to microglia (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-nuclei RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei from patients and controls were submitted to targeted deep-DNA sequencing.
claims.source: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei (glia/stromal cells) from patients and controls (Figure 1A) were submitted to targeted hybridization/capture and deep-DNA targeted sequencing (TDS, Figure 1D, see Materials and methods), at mean coverage of ~1100 x (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), for a panel of 716 genes (3.43 Mb, referred to below as BRAIN-PACT) which included genes reported to carry somatic variants in clonal proliferative disorders (n=576 genes) Cheng et al., 2015; Durham et al., 2019 or that have been reported to be associated with neurodegenerativediseases (n=140) (Bras et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2014; Karch et al., 2014; Karch and Goate, 2015; Turner et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Kouri et al., 2015; Scholz and Bras, 2015; Nalls et al., 2014; Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology and is shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The mean sequencing coverage was approximately 1100x.
claims.source: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei (glia/stromal cells) from patients and controls (Figure 1A) were submitted to targeted hybridization/capture and deep-DNA targeted sequencing (TDS, Figure 1D, see Materials and methods), at mean coverage of ~1100 x (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), for a panel of 716 genes (3.43 Mb, referred to below as BRAIN-PACT) which included genes reported to carry somatic variants in clonal proliferative disorders (n=576 genes) Cheng et al., 2015; Durham et al., 2019 or that have been reported to be associated with neurodegenerativediseases (n=140) (Bras et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2014; Karch et al., 2014; Karch and Goate, 2015; Turner et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Kouri et al., 2015; Scholz and Bras, 2015; Nalls et al., 2014; Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a technical detail of the sequencing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The BRAIN-PACT panel included 716 genes covering 3.43 Mb.
claims.source: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei (glia/stromal cells) from patients and controls (Figure 1A) were submitted to targeted hybridization/capture and deep-DNA targeted sequencing (TDS, Figure 1D, see Materials and methods), at mean coverage of ~1100 x (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), for a panel of 716 genes (3.43 Mb, referred to below as BRAIN-PACT) which included genes reported to carry somatic variants in clonal proliferative disorders (n=576 genes) Cheng et al., 2015; Durham et al., 2019 or that have been reported to be associated with neurodegenerativediseases (n=140) (Bras et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2014; Karch et al., 2014; Karch and Goate, 2015; Turner et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Kouri et al., 2015; Scholz and Bras, 2015; Nalls et al., 2014; Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the gene panel used for sequencing.

claims.claim: Variant calling using ShearwaterML and Mutect1 identified 826 somatic single-nucleotide-variations at an allelic frequency >0.3%.
claims.source: After QC and filtering of germline variants, variant calling using ShearwaterML, and a curated Mutect1 analysis identified 826 somatic synonymous and non-synonymous single-nucleotide-variations (SNVs), at an allelic frequency >0.3% (mean 1.3%) in the 744 samples, corresponding to an overall variant burden of 0.3 mut/Mb (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary result from the sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The overall variant burden was 0.3 mutations per megabase.
claims.source: After QC and filtering of germline variants, variant calling using ShearwaterML, and a curated Mutect1 analysis identified 826 somatic synonymous and non-synonymous single-nucleotide-variations (SNVs), at an allelic frequency >0.3% (mean 1.3%) in the 744 samples, corresponding to an overall variant burden of 0.3 mut/Mb (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Droplet digital-PCR confirmed approximately 90% of tested variants.
claims.source: Droplet digital-PCR performed on pre-amplification DNA for ~10% of the 760 unique SNV was positive in 90% of cases (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This validation data is shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: 96 unique SNVs were classified as pathogenic.
claims.source: After annotation using the OncoKB Chakravarty et al., 2017 and ClinVar (Landrum et al., 2014) databases for disease-associated or causative variants (Figure 2D and F; Supplementary file 3), 96 unique SNV were classified as Pathogenic (P)-SNV.
claims.evidence: This is based on annotation using established databases as shown in Figure 2D and F.

claims.claim: 95% of tested pathogenic SNVs were confirmed by droplet digital-PCR.
claims.source: 40% of these P-SNV were tested by droplet digital-PCR and confirmed in 95% of cases (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This validation data is shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Most SNVs and pathogenic SNVs were cell-type or tissue-specific.
claims.source: A venn-diagram analysis of SNVs detected in PU.1+, NeuN+, DN, and blood samples indicated that most (>90%) SNV and P-SNV were cell-type or tissue-specific, with ~5% of SNV and ~8% of P-SNV shared between the blood and brain of individual donors (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Approximately 5% of SNVs and 8% of pathogenic SNVs were shared between blood and brain.
claims.source: A venn-diagram analysis of SNVs detected in PU.1+, NeuN+, DN, and blood samples indicated that most (>90%) SNV and P-SNV were cell-type or tissue-specific, with ~5% of SNV and ~8% of P-SNV shared between the blood and brain of individual donors (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Infiltrating myeloid cells of peripheral origin account for approximately 5% of microglia somatic diversity.
claims.source: These data indicate that targeted deep-sequencing of purified nuclei allows to detect of clonal mosaic variants with high sensitivity and specificity. In addition, 'bar-coding' of clonal variants across tissues suggests that infiltrating myeloid cells of peripheral origin account for ~5% of microglia somatic diversity, and therefore that blood clones have a detectable but minor contribution to microglia, consistent with its local maintenance and proliferation (Askew et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data on shared variants between blood and brain.

claims.claim: Clonal diversity of blood and PU.1+ nuclei was higher than for DN and neurons.
claims.source: Somatic clonal diversity of the different cell types, as evaluated by the SNV/megabase burden was higher in blood (1 mut/Mb) and PU.1+ nuclei (0.5 mut/Mb) than for DN and neurons (0.18 mut/Mb) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The SNV/mb burden of blood and PU.1+ nuclei increased as a function of age.
claims.source: The SNV/mb burden of blood and PU.1+ nuclei increased as a function of age (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 3) as previously reported for proliferating cells (Martincorena et al., 2015; Martincorena et al., 2018; Jaiswal et al., 2014; Genovese et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with published literature.

claims.claim: The SNV/mb burden of blood cells from age-matched controls was higher than for AD patients.
claims.source: Interestingly, the SNV/mb burden of blood cells from age-matched controls was higher than for AD patients (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: There was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+, NEUN+, and DN samples from AD patients and age-matched controls.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+, NEUN+, and DN samples from AD patients and age-matched controls (Figure 2B), and between PU.1+ nuclei from the cortex, hippocampus, and brainstem/cerebellum samples (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: There was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+ nuclei from different brain regions.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+, NEUN+, and DN samples from AD patients and age-matched controls (Figure 2B), and between PU.1+ nuclei from the cortex, hippocampus, and brainstem/cerebellum samples (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Clonal hematopoiesis is inversely associated with the risk of AD.
claims.source: This is consistent with recent studies showing that clonal hematopoiesis is associated with a higher risk of several diseases related to ageing such as cardiovascular diseases, but is inversely associated with the risk of AD (Jaiswal and Ebert, 2019; Bouzid et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: Increased pathogenic SNV burden was correlated with age.
claims.source: In contrast to the global SNV burden, increased P-SNV burden was correlated not only with age (Figure 2D), but also with the disease status (AD) (Figure 2E–H).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Increased pathogenic SNV burden was correlated with AD disease status.
claims.source: In contrast to the global SNV burden, increased P-SNV burden was correlated not only with age (Figure 2D), but also with the disease status (AD) (Figure 2E–H).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figures 2E-H.

claims.claim: The pathogenic SNV burden per Mb was selectively and highly enriched in PU.1+ samples from AD patients compared to age-matched controls (p=0.0003).
claims.source: The P-SNV burden per Mb was selectively and highly enriched in PU.1+ samples from AD patients in comparison to age-matched controls (p=0.0003, Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This statistical comparison is shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The pathogenic SNV/Mb burden was similar between brain regions within each group.
claims.source: Analysis of PU1+ P-SNV/Mb burden per brains region indicated that the P-SNV/Mb burden was similar between brain regions within each group (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and therefore attributable to AD status rather than sampling bias.
claims.evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Microglial clones carrying pathogenic SNVs were enriched in the brain of AD patients compared to age-matched controls.
claims.source: Analysis of mutational load per donor confirmed that microglial clones carrying P-SNV were enriched in the brain of AD patients in comparison to age-matched controls (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: A logistic regression analysis confirmed the association between the presence of pathogenic SNVs in PU.1+ nuclei and AD after adjusting for sex and age (OR = 7; p=0.0035).
claims.source: Despite the relatively modest cohort size, a logistic regression analysis confirmed the association between the presence of P-SNVs in PU.1+ nuclei and AD after adjusting for sex and age (OR = 7; p=0.0035, Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This statistical analysis is shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: A mixed-effects linear regression model showed an excess of pathogenic SNVs in AD independently of the effect of age (p=0.0215).
claims.source: A mixed-effects linear regression model analysis also showed an excess of P-SNVs in AD independently of the effect of age (p=0.0215) (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This statistical analysis is shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Genes targeted by pathogenic SNVs were all expressed in microglia.
claims.source: In addition, genes targeted by P-SNV were all expressed in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 3) and the analysis of P-SNV/Mb mutational load restricted to genes that are not expressed in microglia did not show an enrichment of candidate pathogenic variants in AD patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Analysis of pathogenic SNV/Mb mutational load restricted to genes not expressed in microglia did not show enrichment in AD patients.
claims.source: In addition, genes targeted by P-SNV were all expressed in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 3) and the analysis of P-SNV/Mb mutational load restricted to genes that are not expressed in microglia did not show an enrichment of candidate pathogenic variants in AD patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This control analysis is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The most significant pathways enriched for genes carrying pathogenic SNVs in microglia from AD patients were the receptor tyrosine kinase/MAP-Kinase pathways.
claims.source: Pathways analysis of genes carrying P-SNV in microglia from AD patients, against the background of the 716 genes sequenced, showed that the most significant pathways enriched were the receptor tyrosine kinase/MAP-Kinase pathways (Reactome, GO, and canonical pathways, Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4), corresponding to pathogenic/oncogenic variants in 6 of the 15 genes of the classical MAPK pathway (Rauen, 2013) (CBL, BRAF, RIT1, NF1, PTPN11, KRAS), TEK, and the KEGG Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) pathway, which includes the former plus SMAD5 and TP53 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This pathway analysis is shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: Pathogenic/oncogenic variants were found in 6 of the 15 genes of the classical MAPK pathway in AD patients.
claims.source: Pathways analysis of genes carrying P-SNV in microglia from AD patients, against the background of the 716 genes sequenced, showed that the most significant pathways enriched were the receptor tyrosine kinase/MAP-Kinase pathways (Reactome, GO, and canonical pathways, Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4), corresponding to pathogenic/oncogenic variants in 6 of the 15 genes of the classical MAPK pathway (Rauen, 2013) (CBL, BRAF, RIT1, NF1, PTPN11, KRAS), TEK, and the KEGG Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) pathway, which includes the former plus SMAD5 and TP53 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: Mutational load for MAPK genes was significantly higher in AD patients compared to age-matched controls.
claims.source: Mutational load for MAPK genes was significantly higher in AD patients in comparison to age-matched control (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Pathogenic SNVs targeting genes of the classical RTK/MAPK pathway were detected in PU.1+ samples from approximately 25% of AD patients tested (p=0.0145 vs age-matched controls).
claims.source: P-SNV targeting genes of the classical RTK/MAPK pathway (Figure 3C) were detected in the PU.1+ samples from ~25% of the AD patients tested (p=0.0145 vs age-matched controls, Figure 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Six patients (13% of AD patients) carried recurrent pathogenic SNVs in the RING domain of CBL.
claims.source: Strikingly, half of these patients (six patients, 13% of AD patients in this series) carried recurrent P-SNV in the RING domain of CBL (Schnittger et al., 2012; Fernandes et al., 2010; Sargin et al., 2007; Dunbar et al., 2008; Bernard et al., 2014; Loh et al., 2009; Grand et al., 2009; Klampfl et al., 2013; Niemeyer et al., 2010; Javadi et al., 2013; Ogawa, 2019; Figure 3B–E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B-E.

claims.claim: Two patients presented with pathogenic SNVs in the Switch II domain of RIT1.
claims.source: Two additional patients presented with P-SNV in the Switch II domain of RIT1 (Gómez-Seguí et al., 2013; Figure 3B–F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B-F.

claims.claim: CBL RING-domain variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to EGF.
claims.source: We confirmed that CBL RING-domain variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to EGF upon expression of HA-tagged WT or mutant alleles in HEK293T cells (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This functional validation is shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to FBS in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: As in the case of CBL variants, the 2 RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to FBS in HEK293T cells expressing these mutant alleles (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This functional validation is shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Approximately 27% of AD patients in this series present with microglial clones carrying one or several oncogenic variants that activate the RTK/MAPK pathway.
claims.source: These data altogether indicate that a subset of AD patients (12/45, ~27% of this series) present with microglial clones carrying one or several oncogenic variants that activate the RTK/MAPK pathway, and are characterized by recurrent oncogenic variants in CBL and RIT1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings on MAPK pathway variants.

claims.claim: The allelic frequencies of MAPK activating variants in brain samples from AD patients range from approximately 1-6% in microglia.
claims.source: The allelic frequencies at which MAPK activating variants are detected in brain samples from AD patients range from ~1–6% in microglia (Figure 3G), which correspond to mutant clones representing 2 to 12% of all microglia in these samples, assuming heterozygosity.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The allelic frequency range of MAPK activating variants in AD patients is comparable to that observed for BRAFV600E in microglia from histiocytosis patients.
claims.source: This range of allelic frequency is frequently observed for the MAPK-activating BRAFV600E variant in microglia isolated from brain samples of six patients diagnosed with BRAFV600E+ histiocytosis, a rare clonal myeloid disorder associated with neurodegeneration (Mass et al., 2017; Boyd et al., 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020; Diamond et al., 2016; Héritier et al., 2018; Figure 3G and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: CBL variants increased ERK phosphorylation upon lentiviral transduction in BV2 murine microglial cells.
claims.source: CBL variants increased ERK phosphorylation upon lentiviral transduction in BV2 murine microglial cells (Blasi et al., 1990; Henn et al., 2009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: MAC lines expressing CBL, RIT1, KRAS, and PTPN11 variants presented with increased ERK phosphorylation and/or increased proliferation.
claims.source: MAC lines expressing CBL, RIT1, KRAS, and PTPN11 variants presented with increased ERK phosphorylation and/or increontrols, as measured by Western immunoblotting and EdU incorporation (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Hallmark and KEGG pathway analysis of RNAseq data from mutant MAC lines showed increased RAS, TNF, IL6, JAK STAT signaling, complement, inflammatory responses, and mTOR pathway activation signatures.
claims.source: In addition, Hallmark and KEGG pathway analysis of RNAseq data from control and mutant lines showed increased RAS, TNF, IL6, and JAK STAT signaling, complement, inflammatory responses, and mTOR pathway activation signatures in mutants (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7.

claims.claim: CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells were larger and presented with more lamellipodia than isogenic controls.
claims.source: However, CBL404C/Y cells were larger and presented with more lamellipodia, resulting in an amoeboid morphology less frequently observed in isogenic controls (Figure 4D and E), and their proliferation rate was slightly increased, as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figures 4D and E.

claims.claim: The proliferation rate of CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells was slightly increased compared to isogenic controls.
claims.source: However, CBL404C/Y cells were larger and presented with more lamellipodia, resulting in an amoeboid morphology less frequently observed in isogenic controls (Figure 4D and E), and their proliferation rate was slightly increased, as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: ERK phosphorylation after stimulation with CSF-1 was increased by approximately twofold in CBL404C/Y cells compared to isogenic WT.
claims.source: Moreover CBL404C/Y cells cultured in CSF1-supplemented medium also presented with a higher basal pERK level than control when restimulated with CSF1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), and ERK phosphorylation after stimulation of starved microglia-like cells with CSF-1 was increased by ~ twofold in comparison to isogenic WT (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Heterozygosity for a CBLC404Y allele is sufficient to activate human microglia-like cells increasing their proliferation and ERK activation.
claims.source: Altogether, these results showed that heterozygosity for a CBLC404Y allele is sufficient to activate human microglia-like cells increasing their proliferation and ERK activation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments on CBL404C/Y cells.

claims.claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analyses of RNAseq comparing CBL404C/Y and isogenic CBL404C/C microglia-like cells showed upregulation of Glycolysis, Oxidative Phosphorylation, and mTORC1 signatures.
claims.source: Gene Set Enrichment Analyses (GSEA) of RNAseq comparing CBL404C/Y and isogenic CBL404C/C microglia-like cells showed upregulation of Glycolysis, Oxidative Phosphorylation, and mTORC1 signatures, indicating increased metabolism and energy consumption by the mutant cells (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8.

claims.claim: CBL404C/Y cells upregulated complement, TNF, and JAK STAT signaling and inflammatory signatures.
claims.source: In addition, as observed in MAC lines, CBL404C/Y cells upregulated complement, TNF, and JAK STAT signaling and inflammatory signatures (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 8; Ghosh et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8.

claims.claim: Increased production of TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, C3, and complement Factor H by CBL404C/Y cells was confirmed by ELISA.
claims.source: Increased production of TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, C3, and complement Factor H (CFH) by CBL404C/Y cells was confirmed by ELISA (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells presented with signatures associated with neurodegenerative disorders from the KEGG database.
claims.source: In addition, CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells also presented with signatures from the KEGG database associated with neurodegenerative disorders (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 8), and for the recently published human microglia AD scRNA-seq signature, obtained by analysis of 24 sporadic AD patients and 24 controls (Mathys et al., 2019; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8.

claims.claim: CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells showed enrichment for the human AD-microglia snRNA-seq signature.
claims.source: In addition, CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells also presented with signatures from the KEGG database associated with neurodegenerative disorders (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 8), and for the recently published human microglia AD scRNA-seq signature, obtained by analysis of 24 sporadic AD patients and 24 controls (Mathys et al., 2019; Figure 5C).

results.result: The study cohort consisted of 45 AD patients and 44 controls (including 27 age-matched), with APOE frequencies comparable to published data. Targeted deep sequencing of 744 samples (PU.1+, NeuN+, DN nuclei, and blood) was performed using a 716-gene panel at ~1100x coverage, with ~94% of PU.1+ nuclei confirmed as microglia by snRNA-seq.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 describe the study design, cohort characteristics, and technical methodology. The cohort composition, APOE distribution, sequencing coverage, and microglia purity are well-documented with appropriate validation (Figure 1, supplementary data). These foundational methodological claims are adequately supported.

results.result: Variant calling identified 826 somatic SNVs (0.3 mut/Mb) with 90% validation by ddPCR. Of these, 96 were classified as pathogenic (P-SNV) with 95% validation rate. Most variants (>90%) were cell-type specific, with only ~5% of SNVs and ~8% of P-SNVs shared between blood and brain, suggesting infiltrating peripheral myeloid cells account for ~5% of microglia somatic diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 present the variant detection results with strong validation data. The high ddPCR confirmation rates (90% for all SNVs, 95% for P-SNVs) and cell-type specificity analysis support the technical quality. The inference about peripheral cell contribution (C46) is reasonable given the barcode analysis, though it assumes all shared variants originate from peripheral infiltration.

results.result: Somatic variant burden was higher in blood (1 mut/Mb) and PU.1+ nuclei (0.5 mut/Mb) than in DN and neurons (0.18 mut/Mb), and increased with age in blood and microglia. Blood SNV burden was higher in controls than AD patients, while brain cell SNV burden showed no difference between AD and controls across cell types or brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 describe overall mutational burden patterns. The age correlation (C48) is consistent with known biology of proliferating cells. The finding of higher blood SNV burden in controls vs AD (C49) is interesting and statistically supported (Figure 2B), though the biological interpretation requires caution as controls died of other causes including cancer.

results.result: Pathogenic SNV (P-SNV) burden correlated with both age and AD status, with selective enrichment in PU.1+ samples from AD patients vs controls (p=0.0003). This association was confirmed by logistic regression (OR=7, p=0.0035) and mixed-effects modeling (p=0.0215), and was consistent across brain regions, indicating disease-specific rather than sampling-related enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 present the key finding of pathogenic variant enrichment in AD microglia. Multiple statistical approaches converge on significant association (p=0.0003, OR=7, mixed-effects p=0.0215). The consistency across brain regions (C56) strengthens the conclusion. However, the modest cohort size (n=45 AD, n=27 age-matched controls) and multiple testing considerations warrant cautious interpretation of effect sizes.

results.result: All genes targeted by pathogenic SNVs were expressed in microglia, and analysis restricted to genes not expressed in microglia showed no enrichment of pathogenic variants in AD patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 provide important negative control evidence. The finding that P-SNV enrichment is specific to microglia-expressed genes (C60) and absent in non-expressed genes (C61) strengthens the biological relevance of the findings. This control analysis is well-designed and supports specificity.

results.result: Pathway analysis revealed enrichment of pathogenic variants in the RTK/MAPK pathway, with variants in 6 of 15 classical MAPK genes (CBL, BRAF, RIT1, NF1, PTPN11, KRAS) detected in ~25% of AD patients (p=0.0145 vs controls). Notably, 6 patients (13%) carried recurrent CBL RING-domain mutations, and 2 patients had RIT1 Switch II domain variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67, C70 identify MAPK pathway enrichment as the primary mechanistic finding. The pathway analysis is appropriately controlled (716-gene background), and the recurrence of CBL variants in 6/45 patients (13%) is striking. The p=0.0145 for MAPK pathway enrichment is significant, though multiple pathway testing should be considered. The recurrent CBL mutations provide strong evidence for selection.

results.result: Functional validation in HEK293T cells demonstrated that CBL RING-domain variants and RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to EGF and FBS, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 provide functional validation of variant pathogenicity. Western blot data (Figure 3E-F) demonstrate increased ERK phosphorylation for patient-derived variants. However, validation is performed in HEK293T cells rather than microglia, and only tests acute signaling responses. The functional relevance in physiological microglia context requires additional validation.

results.result: MAPK-activating variants in AD patients were detected at allelic frequencies of ~1-6% in microglia (corresponding to 2-12% of microglia assuming heterozygosity), comparable to BRAFV600E frequencies observed in microglia from histiocytosis patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 contextualize the variant allelic frequencies. The comparison to histiocytosis (C72) is appropriate given the known association with neurodegeneration. The allelic frequency range (1-6%) is consistent with clonal expansion but below typical cancer frequencies, which is biologically plausible for a non-malignant clonal disorder.

results.result: In murine microglial cell lines (BV2) and CSF-1-dependent macrophages (MAC), expression of CBL, RIT1, KRAS, and PTPN11 variants increased ERK phosphorylation and/or proliferation, and RNA-seq showed upregulation of RAS, TNF, IL6, JAK-STAT signaling, complement, inflammatory responses, and mTOR pathway signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 demonstrate functional consequences in mouse cell lines. Western blot and EdU incorporation data (Figure 4A) support increased signaling and proliferation. RNA-seq pathway analysis (Figure 4B) shows inflammatory signatures. However, these are immortalized/transformed mouse lines, which may not fully recapitulate primary human microglia biology. The BV2 line is v-Raf immortalized, potentially confounding MAPK pathway studies.

results.result: Human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells heterozygous for CBL C404Y showed increased size, lamellipodia, amoeboid morphology, slightly increased proliferation, and ~2-fold increased ERK phosphorylation upon CSF-1 stimulation compared to isogenic controls, demonstrating that heterozygosity for CBLC404Y is sufficient to activate human microglia-like cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 provide critical validation in human cells with physiological heterozygosity. The use of prime-edited isogenic iPSC lines is rigorous. Morphological changes (Figure 4D-E), proliferation (Figure 4F), and ERK activation (Figure 4G) are documented. However, these are iPSC-derived cells that may not fully recapitulate mature brain microglia. The 'slightly increased' proliferation (C77) suggests modest effects.

results.result: RNA-seq of CBL404C/Y iPSC-derived microglia showed upregulation of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, mTORC1, complement, TNF, JAK-STAT signaling, inflammatory signatures, KEGG neurodegenerative disease signatures, and the human AD-microglia signature. ELISA confirmed increased production of TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, C3, and complement Factor H, indicating heterozygosity for CBLC404Y drives a neuroinflammatory/AD signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 demonstrate transcriptional and protein-level inflammatory responses. GSEA shows enrichment for AD-associated signatures (Figure 5A-C), and ELISA confirms cytokine production (Figure 5B). The convergence of multiple inflammatory pathways and validation at protein level strengthens conclusions. However, in vitro culture conditions may not fully replicate in vivo inflammatory milieu. The n=3-4 replicates for ELISA is modest.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of microglia from patients with MAPK variants showed enrichment for inflammatory, TNF, mTOR, oxidative phosphorylation, and glycolysis signatures, particularly in clusters 2 and 2B. KRAS A59G variant reads were detected in cluster 2/2B from patient AD52, supporting that patient microglial clones carrying pathogenic mutations are associated with metabolic and neuroinflammatory signatures in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 attempt to validate in vitro findings in patient samples. The snRNA-seq shows enrichment of inflammatory signatures in variant-carrying patients (Figure 5D-E). However, the analysis is limited to 5 samples from 4 donors, with only 2 AD patients carrying variants. Detection of variant reads at single-cell level (C88) is notable but challenging given low VAF and sequencing depth. The small sample size and difficulty distinguishing cause vs. effect limit certainty.

results.result: Microglia from 45 AD patients are selectively enriched for pathogenic/oncogenic variants absent from blood, glia, or neurons compared to 44 controls. These variants predominantly target the MAPK pathway and include recurrent CBL RING-domain mutations, which promote microglial proliferation, activation, and neuroinflammatory transcriptional programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C90-C92 summarize the main findings. The enrichment of microglia-specific pathogenic variants in AD (p=0.0003, OR=7) is well-supported by multiple statistical approaches. MAPK pathway enrichment and CBL recurrence are documented. Cell-type specificity is demonstrated. However, causality vs. consequence cannot be definitively established from this cross-sectional study. The 'promote' language in C92 implies causation that requires longitudinal or interventional data.

results.result: Heterozygous expression of pathogenic CBL variant in human microglia-like cells was sufficient to drive a transcriptional program associated with increased metabolic activity and neurotoxic inflammatory response, also observed in microglia from patients with MAPK-activating variants.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 integrates in vitro and patient data. The iPSC-derived cell experiments (C80-C85) demonstrate sufficiency of heterozygous CBL variant for inflammatory phenotype. Patient snRNA-seq (C86-C87) shows similar signatures. However, 'sufficient' is strong language given that in vitro systems may not capture all regulatory mechanisms. The patient validation is limited by small sample size (n=2 variant carriers).

results.result: The association between AD and MAPK pathway variants is consistent with prior whole-exome sequencing showing MAPK enrichment in AD brain tissue. Additionally, MAPK-activating variants in tissue macrophages cause histiocytosis with neurodegeneration, and BRAFV600E expression in mouse microglia causes neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 contextualize findings with prior literature. The consistency with Park et al. 2019 (C94) supports reproducibility despite different methods. The histiocytosis connection (C95) and mouse BRAFV600E model (C96) provide mechanistic precedent. However, these are citations to prior work rather than new findings. The relevance of histiocytosis (a rare clonal disorder) to sporadic AD requires careful interpretation.

results.result: The allelic frequencies of pathogenic variants in AD patients are within the range observed in histiocytosis and autoimmune diseases. The RAS/MAPK pathway is involved in microglia proliferation, activation, inflammatory response, and AD pathogenesis, with activation proposed as an early event in AD. Neuroinflammation is an early and critical event in AD, and APOE4, the main genetic risk factor, increases inflammatory responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 provide biological context through literature citations. The allelic frequency comparison (C97) is appropriate. The role of MAPK in microglia function (C98) and AD pathogenesis (C99) is well-established in cited literature. The emphasis on neuroinflammation (C100) and APOE4 (C101) contextualizes the findings. These are primarily literature-based contextual claims rather than new findings.

results.result: The contributing role of MAPK-activating variants could be comparable to APOE4, and APOE4 allele frequency is lower in patients with pathogenic variants (34%) than without (53%), though this difference did not reach significance.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 propose a relationship between MAPK variants and APOE4. The observation of lower APOE4 frequency in variant carriers (34% vs 53%) is interesting but non-significant (C103). The speculation about comparable contribution to APOE4 (C102) is not supported by statistical evidence or mechanistic data. The sample size (n=23 variant carriers) is insufficient to detect this difference. This remains a hypothesis requiring validation.

results.result: Microglia variants are frequently absent from blood, and the DNA sequencing barcode approach does not support massive blood cell infiltration or replacement of the microglia pool, but instead is consistent with local microglia maintenance and proliferation. This is consistent with studies showing clonal hematopoiesis is inversely associated with AD risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 address the origin of microglial variants. The low frequency of shared variants between blood and brain (5-8%, C45) supports local origin rather than peripheral infiltration. The consistency with microglia biology literature (C105) and inverse association of clonal hematopoiesis with AD (C106) strengthens the interpretation. However, the barcode approach cannot definitively exclude all peripheral contribution, particularly for variants arising in early hematopoietic progenitors.

results.result: The association of microglia clones carrying pathogenic variants with AD is not due to overall increased microglia mutational load in AD. Together with evidence that pathogenic variants drive neuroinflammation, these data suggest clones could contribute to AD pathogenesis with other genetic and environmental factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 distinguish pathogenic variant enrichment from general mutational burden. The finding that overall SNV burden is similar between AD and controls (C50) while P-SNV burden is elevated (C55) supports specificity (C107). The suggestion of contribution to pathogenesis (C108) is appropriately cautious ('could contribute', 'suggest') given the cross-sectional design. However, causality cannot be established without longitudinal or interventional studies.

results.result: Lewy bodies, amyloid angiopathy, tauopathy, or alpha synucleinopathy were equally distributed among AD patients with or without microglia clones carrying MAPK-activating variants.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 reports no association between MAPK variants and specific AD pathological features. This negative finding is important for understanding the relationship between microglial clones and AD subtypes. The data are presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. However, the sample size for subgroup analysis is limited, and statistical power to detect associations may be insufficient.

results.result: The natural history of microglial clones is difficult to study in humans. Microglial expression of MAPK-activating variants causes neurodegeneration in mice, suggesting AD-associated neuroinflammatory microglial clones may contribute to neurodegeneration in patients. Clones may be present at onset contributing to early disease, or may appear/be selected later during disease progression in the inflammatory milieu.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C28, C110-C113 discuss temporal dynamics and causality. The mouse model data (C8, C28) from prior work (Mass et al. 2017) provides mechanistic support but cannot establish timing in human disease. The acknowledgment of difficulty studying natural history (C110) is appropriate. The alternative hypotheses about early vs. late emergence (C111-C112) are reasonable but speculative. The cross-sectional design cannot distinguish cause from consequence or determine when clones arise. Longitudinal studies would be required.

results.result: Background claims establishing the context of somatic mosaicism, AD epidemiology, genetic risk factors (APOE4, GWAS variants), prior evidence of mosaicism in AD brain tissue, and the role of microglia in AD pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C31, C33, C52 provide literature-based background and context. These are primarily citations to established knowledge and prior studies. The claims accurately represent the cited literature regarding AD prevalence, genetic risk factors, somatic mosaicism, and microglia biology. C25 appropriately identifies limitations of prior studies (lack of cellular resolution), motivating the current work. These contextual claims are well-supported by citations.

results.result: The study examined post-mortem brain samples and blood from 45 AD patients and 44 controls, using targeted deep sequencing of 744 samples across multiple cell types (PU.1+, NeuN+, DN, blood) with a BRAIN-PACT panel of 716 genes at ~1100x coverage. APOE allele frequencies were comparable to published series, and ~94% of PU.1+ nuclei corresponded to microglia.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accepted the study design and methodology without critique. Reviewer 3 explicitly noted 'the authors used two methods to identify mosaic mutations' as a strength, and Reviewer 2 stated 'great care was taken to identify the limitations.' The cohort characterization and technical approach are treated as sound.

results.result: Variant calling identified 826 somatic SNVs (0.3 mut/Mb burden), with ~90% validated by ddPCR. Of these, 96 were classified as pathogenic (P-SNVs), with 95% validation rate. Most variants were cell-type specific, with only ~5% of SNVs and ~8% of P-SNVs shared between blood and brain, suggesting infiltrating myeloid cells account for ~5% of microglia somatic diversity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted 'extensive molecular and functional validation of mutation candidates' as a strength. Reviewer 2 stated 'the over-activation of the cells in vitro is convincing.' The validation rates and cell-type specificity findings are not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Overall SNV burden was higher in blood and PU.1+ nuclei than in DN and neurons, and increased with age in proliferating cells. Interestingly, blood SNV burden was higher in controls than AD patients, consistent with inverse association between clonal hematopoiesis and AD risk. No difference in SNV burden was observed between AD and controls in brain cell types or across brain regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly noted 'the study supports an enrichment of P-SNVs in several genes...and nicely separates this from SNVs associated with clonal hematopoiesis in the peripheral blood.' No reviewer challenged these findings about overall SNV burden patterns.

results.result: Pathogenic SNV (P-SNV) burden was selectively enriched in PU.1+ samples from AD patients compared to age-matched controls (p=0.0003), independent of age effects (p=0.0215), with an odds ratio of 7 (p=0.0035). This enrichment was consistent across brain regions and specific to genes expressed in microglia. The association remained significant after adjusting for sex and age.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is compelling' and Reviewer 3 noted 'their data strongly suggest that mosaic MAPK mutations in microglia are associated with AD.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'the sample size...is small, reflected in the relatively modest effect sizes and p-values' but concluded this 'weakness is partially ameliorated by the authors' extensive molecular and functional validation.'

results.result: Pathway analysis revealed that P-SNVs in AD microglia preferentially targeted the RTK/MAPK pathway, with pathogenic variants in 6 of 15 classical MAPK genes detected in ~25% of AD patients (p=0.0145 vs controls). Strikingly, 6 patients (13%) carried recurrent CBL RING-domain mutations, and 2 patients had RIT1 Switch II domain mutations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 highlighted 'they identified P-SNVs in microglia of AD patients located within the ring domain of CBL' and noted 'an in depth analysis in re-occurring P-SNVs' as a strength. Reviewer 3 stated 'the authors report a striking enrichment for mutations in the gene CBL' and noted agreement between targeted sequencing and WES methods.

results.result: Functional validation showed that CBL RING-domain and RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK/ERK phosphorylation in multiple cell systems (HEK293T, BV2 murine microglia, MAC lines), with increased proliferation in cells expressing these variants.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'they further provide mechanistic insights how these variants result in MAPK over-activation...in HEK cells, BV2 cells, MAC cells and human microglia-like cells in vitro. The over-activation of the cells in vitro is convincing.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors demonstrated in several in vitro systems that many mutations they identified in MAPK genes activate MAPK signaling' as a strength.

results.result: iPSC-derived microglia-like cells heterozygous for CBL404C/Y showed increased ERK phosphorylation (~2-fold), slightly increased proliferation, altered morphology, and upregulation of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, mTORC1, inflammatory signatures (TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, complement), and AD-associated transcriptional signatures, demonstrating that heterozygosity for CBLC404Y is sufficient to drive a neuroinflammatory/AD phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 emphasized 'they further provide mechanistic insights how these variants result in MAPK over-activation and subsequently in a pro-inflammatory phenotype in human microglia-like cells in vitro.' Reviewer 3 noted this as a strength, stating 'the authors demonstrated in several in vitro systems' the functional consequences of mutations.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of patient microglia showed that samples from patients carrying MAPK variants were enriched for inflammatory, TNF, mTOR, oxidative phosphorylation, and glycolysis signatures, particularly in clusters 2 and 2B. Variant reads were detected at single-cell resolution, supporting that patient microglial clones carrying pathogenic mutations are associated with metabolic and neuroinflammatory signatures in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 stated 'the authors showed that in some human brain samples, single-cell gene expression analysis revealed that cells bearing a mosaic MAPK pathway mutation displayed dysregulated inflammatory signaling...This single-cell analysis was in agreement with their in vitro analyses.' This concordance between in vitro and patient data is treated as a strength.

results.result: Approximately 27% of AD patients presented with microglial clones carrying oncogenic MAPK pathway variants at allelic frequencies of 1-6% (representing 2-12% of microglia), comparable to frequencies in histiocytosis patients. These variants were predominantly absent from blood, glia, or neurons, and heterozygous expression was sufficient to drive neuroinflammatory transcriptional programs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is compelling, with the authors employing a multi-faceted approach to identify an enrichment of potentially pathogenic somatic mutations in Alzheimer's disease microglia.' Reviewer 2 noted 'great care was taken to identify the limitations of the possible conclusions and to make careful conclusions...they highlight that the pathway proposed to be affected may be an explanation for a subset of AD patients.'

results.result: The authors suggest that AD-associated neuroinflammatory microglial clones may contribute to the neurodegenerative process in patients, though they acknowledge the natural history is difficult to establish and it remains unclear whether clones are present at disease onset or selected later during disease progression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'they emphasize that it is yet unclear whether this accumulation of pathological SNVs is a cause or consequence of disease progression' and stated 'some points especially regarding the clear connection of the seen somatic variants in microglia with a potential role in disease progression remain unanswered.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'this study cannot conclude whether microglial mosaic mutations cause AD or are an effect of AD.'

results.result: The findings are consistent with prior literature showing MAPK pathway enrichment in AD brain tissue, the role of MAPK variants in histiocytosis-associated neurodegeneration, mouse models demonstrating BRAFV600E causes neurodegeneration, and the established role of neuroinflammation and APOE4 in AD pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted 'MAPK has previously been implicated in AD neuroinflammation in the literature' and stated 'the authors' previous work shows that a genetic mouse model of mosaic BRAF activation in macrophages (including microglia) displays a neurodegenerative phenotype similar to AD' as important context. These contextual claims are accepted without challenge.

results.result: The authors note that APOE4 allele frequency was lower in patients with pathogenic variants (34%) than without (53%), though not statistically significant. Microglia variants were frequently absent from blood, consistent with local microglia maintenance rather than blood cell infiltration. The association with AD was not due to overall increased mutational load, and pathological features were equally distributed regardless of variant status.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the study supports an enrichment of P-SNVs in several genes...and nicely separates this from SNVs associated with clonal hematopoiesis in the peripheral blood' and noted 'the authors further acknowledged that several age matched control patients were diagnosed with cancer...and carefully dissected the occurring SNVs.' These observations are treated as careful, appropriate analyses.

results.result: Background claims about somatic mosaicism, AD epidemiology, germline risk factors (APOE4, GWAS variants), prior studies on somatic variants in AD, microglia biology, and the knowledge gap regarding microglial somatic clones in neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: These are introductory/background claims establishing context and rationale. Reviewer 3 explicitly validated this framing, stating 'the current state of the AD and somatic mutation fields puts this work into context' and describing the rationale as sound. No reviewer challenged these background statements.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on study design and methodology (C32-C38). Both evaluations find the cohort characterization, technical approach, and validation methods well-supported. Peer reviewers explicitly noted the methodological rigor as a strength.

Complete agreement on variant detection and validation (C39-C46). Both evaluations accept the high ddPCR confirmation rates and cell-type specificity. Peer reviewers highlighted the extensive molecular validation as a strength.

Strong agreement on overall mutational burden patterns (C47-C51, with peer also including C52). Both evaluations support the age correlation and blood SNV findings. Peer reviewers noted the careful separation of microglia SNVs from clonal hematopoiesis.

Agreement on pathogenic variant enrichment in AD microglia (C53-C59), though peer review also includes C3, C60-C61. Both acknowledge statistical significance while noting modest cohort size. Peer reviewers stated evidence is 'compelling' but acknowledged small sample size limitations.

OpenEval addresses negative control evidence (C60-C61) separately, while peer review groups this with the main enrichment findings (C3, C53-C61). Both evaluations support the specificity demonstrated by these controls.

Strong agreement on MAPK pathway enrichment and CBL recurrence (C62-C67, C70). Both evaluations find the pathway analysis and recurrent mutations compelling. Peer reviewers emphasized the 'striking enrichment' and agreement between methods.

Agreement on functional validation of variant pathogenicity (C68-C69). Both evaluations support the ERK phosphorylation data. OpenEval notes HEK293T cell limitation, while peer reviewers accept the validation across multiple systems as convincing.

OpenEval addresses allelic frequency context (C71-C72) while peer review groups these with broader conclusions (C70-C93). Both evaluations support the histiocytosis comparison and allelic frequency interpretation.

OpenEval evaluates mouse cell line data (C73-C75) separately, while peer review groups functional validation across systems (C68-C69, C73-C74). Both support the findings but OpenEval explicitly notes BV2 cell line limitations.

Agreement on iPSC-derived human cell validation (C76-C79). OpenEval notes 'slightly increased' proliferation suggests modest effects, while peer reviewers emphasize the convincing nature of over-activation across multiple systems including human microglia-like cells.

Strong agreement on inflammatory responses (C80-C85). Both evaluations support the transcriptional and protein-level findings. Peer reviewers highlighted the pro-inflammatory phenotype as convincingly demonstrated across systems.

Perfect claim overlap (C86-C89) but different evaluation outcomes. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to small sample size (n=2 variant carriers) and difficulty distinguishing cause vs. effect. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, emphasizing concordance between in vitro and patient data as a strength.

Agreement on main findings (C3-C5, C90-C92) with appropriate caution. OpenEval notes 'promote' language implies causation requiring longitudinal data. Peer reviewers emphasized careful conclusions and acknowledgment that findings may explain a subset of AD patients.

OpenEval addresses sufficiency claim (C93) separately, noting 'sufficient' is strong language given in vitro limitations. Peer review groups this with broader conclusions, accepting the multi-faceted approach as compelling.
Agreement on literature contextualization (C94-C96). Both evaluations accept these citations to prior work. Peer reviewers noted the MAPK-AD connection and BRAF mouse model provide important context.
Agreement on biological context through literature (C97-C101). Both evaluations support these contextual claims. OpenEval notes these are primarily literature-based rather than new findings.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding MAPK-APOE4 relationship (C102-C103). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting non-significant findings and insufficient sample size. Peer review groups with other observations but accepts the careful analysis.

Agreement on local origin of microglial variants (C104-C106). Both evaluations support the interpretation that variants arise locally rather than from peripheral infiltration. Peer reviewers noted the careful separation from clonal hematopoiesis.

Agreement on distinction between pathogenic variants and general burden (C107-C108). Both evaluations support the specificity of P-SNV enrichment. OpenEval notes appropriate caution about causality given cross-sectional design.
Agreement on negative finding regarding AD pathological features (C109). Both evaluations accept this result while noting limited statistical power for subgroup analysis.

Perfect agreement on uncertainty regarding temporal dynamics and causality (C8-C9, C28, C110-C113). Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN, noting cross-sectional design cannot distinguish cause from consequence. Peer reviewers explicitly stated 'this study cannot conclude whether microglial mosaic mutations cause AD or are an effect of AD.'

Strong agreement on background and contextual claims (C1-C2, C10-C31, C33, C52 in OpenEval; similar set in peer review). Both evaluations support these literature-based claims. Peer reviewers validated the framing and rationale as sound.
